newsitem.title: USA: U.S. High Court hears religious freedom law case.
newsitem.headline: U.S. High Court hears religious freedom law case.

text.p: The Supreme Court on Wednesday was asked to decide whether a 1993 federal law protecting religious freedom violated the separation of church and state guaranteed by the U.S. Constitution.

The arguments came in a challenge to the Religious Freedom Restoration Act, a measure which President Bill Clinton strongly supported. The law bars federal, state and local governments from restricting religious practices unless they can prove a "compelling interest." Even then, they must adopt the least restrictive means possible.

The case arose after the city of Boerne, Texas, near San Antonio, denied a permit to expand a Catholic church because it was within the city's historic district. The archbishop sued, claiming denial of the construction permit violated the law. The city said the law was unconstitutional and a federal judge agreed, but an appeals court upheld it.

Arguing for the city before the high court, Marci Hamilton said the law shifted the balance of power between church and state in favour of religious groups. "This case is not about religious freedom. This case is about federal power."
Ohio State Solicitor Jeffrey Sutton also urged the court to strike down the law, saying the states rather than Congress should and would protect religious rights.
But Douglas Laycock, arguing for the church, said the court should uphold the law. "Congress has always understood it has the right to protect constitutional rights."

U.S. Solicitor General Walter Dellinger also supported the law, saying it was needed to protect the rights of small religious groups that are often treated less favourably than more popular religions.
The justices peppered all four attorneys with questions but gave no clear indication how they might rule. They are expected to decide the case by the end of June.
Besides important church-state issues, the case also raised profound questions about federalism and the separation of powers between the various branches of government.
The First Amendment to the Constitution says Congress shall make make no laws prohibiting the free exercise of religion and can not establish one religion for the nation.
A coalition of more than 60 religious and civil liberties groups urged that the law be upheld in a brief to the court.
But a group of 16 state attorneys general complained the law has been abused by prisoners demanding special food, clothing and other privileges by claiming it was part of their religious beliefs.
